issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Rajan had worked the night shift at the warehouse for nearly two decades, a schedule that had once felt as natural as breathing. Now, at sixty-four, the approach of dusk sent a cold dread through his chest that no amount of logic could dispel. He would stand at the window of his small apartment, watching the orange light fade, and feel his throat tighten. The same time of day. That was when it had happened.

Twelve years ago, during a business trip to a rural region for a supplier audit, Rajan had been taken by a group of men who had mistaken him for a rival. He had been held for six days in a dark, windowless shed. The men had spoken little, but they had brought a snake into the room on the second day-a thick, slow-moving python they let coil near his leg while they laughed. He had not moved. He had not screamed. He had simply frozen, certain that if he flinched, they would let it strike. On the sixth night, around the same hour the sun was now setting, he had managed to slip through a loose board and run until his lungs burned. He had never told the full story to anyone, not even his wife. He had told the police enough, and then he had tried to forget.

But the forgetting never held. At first, it was only the occasional nightmare, a jolt awake in the dark. Over the years, it had grown into a wall of vigilance that separated him from the world. He had stopped sleeping in the same bed as his wife, Priya, because lying in the dark made his skin crawl. He would doze in the living room armchair with the television on, waking at every creak and groan of the building. Going to sleep had become an ordeal he dreaded more than the exhaustion that followed. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down-if he let himself be truly unconscious-something terrible would find him. He was certain that he could not stop bad things from happening, that his own helplessness was a law of the universe.

At work, he had transferred to the day shift, but the damage was done. He could not walk through the warehouse aisles without scanning every shadow, every gap between pallets. He constantly checked his body for signs of injury-a twinge in his knee, a scratch on his arm-as if his own flesh might betray him with a wound he had not noticed. He frequently looked behind him, sometimes stopping mid-stride to turn his head, checking if someone was following. His coworkers had noticed. They joked that he was jumpy. Rajan had stopped eating lunch in the break room because someone had left a nature magazine open to a page about pythons, and the sight of the photograph had sent him to the bathroom to vomit.

He had begun to ask Priya the same question every night, sometimes three or four times: "Am I okay? Tell me I am okay." She would reassure him, her voice patient, but he could see the worry in her eyes. He knew he was wearing her down. He knew he was becoming someone she had to manage rather than love. That knowledge sat inside him like a stone. He had started to think, more and more often, that he was not sure his life was worth living anymore. He did not want to die. He simply could not imagine how to go on living like this-always watching, always waiting, always afraid of his own mind.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a night last month when he had woken in the armchair, drenched in sweat, convinced he could hear the rustle of scales on the floorboards. He had screamed. Priya had run in, and he had pushed her away, shouting at her to stay back. He had seen the fear on her face, and then the hurt. The next morning, she had made an appointment for him. He had not resisted. He was terrified of what he might find in therapy-of what he might have to remember-but he was more terrified of losing her. He was certain that if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it. But he had come anyway, because the alternative felt like drowning.
